written.q: Describe the four levels of the C4 model with what each shows.
written.a: Level 1 System Context: the big picture, who uses the system and what external software systems it interacts with. Level 2 Container: zooms into the system boundary to show high-level technical building blocks (web and mobile apps, API services, databases) and how they communicate over protocols. Level 3 Component: zooms into one container to show its structural components (controllers, repositories, authentication services) and internal interactions. Level 4 Code: zooms into one component to show implementation details such as a class diagram.

written.q: For UniMart, map each growth-crisis symptom to its architectural cause and describe the redesign trade-offs.
written.a: Search leak crashing payments: shared process / failure domain. Payments and Catalog needing different databases: shared database. 3-day copy change: shared deploy pipeline. Conflicting commits: shared codebase. Redesign into Auth, Catalog, Messaging, Orders and Payments, Reviews, Notifications with their own data, API gateway, sync identity checks and async events. Better: independent deploys, fault isolation, database choice, team autonomy. Harder: six pipelines, network failures, no single ACID transaction, service discovery and monitoring, API contracts.

written.q: Explain how the university course registration architecture handles the last-seat race, duplicate registration, read load and email delay.
written.a: Last seat: the registration service performs the capacity check and insert/decrement in one atomic database transaction (row lock or optimistic locking) with a DB constraint as a backstop, so one student succeeds and the other gets 'course full'. Duplicates: a unique (student, course) constraint plus an idempotency key on the POST. Read load: cache the course catalogue (read-heavy, rarely changing) and use a replica. Email: place confirmation on a queue processed by a worker, so registration is not delayed and an email outage does not affect it.

written.q: Outline an architecture for the Zippo ride-hailing app that prevents a repeat of the 3-hour outage and works on 2G.
written.a: Decompose into location, matching/dispatch, trip, pricing, payments (isolated, per country), notifications and a food vertical reusing the driver pool, behind an API gateway. Separate the location pipeline (in-memory geo index, batched eventual writes) from matching so there are no read/write locks. Make payments asynchronous after trip completion with a queue, timeouts, circuit breaker and idempotency keys so a slow gateway never blocks trips and no double charges occur. Autoscale and shed load under surge. For 2G use small payloads, retries with backoff and offline buffering of location in the app. Add tracing for dispute resolution.
